newsitem.title: USA: New rule to expands Alaska air cargo activity.
newsitem.headline: New rule to expands Alaska air cargo activity.

text.p: A new federal policy will allow foreign airlines the authority to sort, store and redirect cargo in Alaska, promising a possible cargo boom at the Anchorage and Fairbanks international airports, officials said on Monday.
The new policy, subject to a 14-day review, was announced on Monday by the U.S. Department of Transportation.
It came in response to an application sent in July from the state for authorization to create an international air cargo hub, an expansion from the current refueling service.
Gov. Tony Knowles and Alaska's U.S. senators hailed the announcement.

"As everybody knows, air cargo is already an important industry for Alaska. We are already America's largest distrubution for foreign cargo. This can expand those opportunities and will be a real job stimulant," Knowles said.

"It's probably the most important thing that has happened in this field in this decade. So we're anxious to have the final approval ... and this will send a clear message to all air carriers that we're open and ready for business," he said.

The new rules would allow on-line cargo transfers between aircraft, changes in size and type of aircraft operated on various flight segments, co-mingling of cargo moving between U.S. and third-country points, interline cargo transfers and cargo storage in Alaksa warehouses.

Air cargo traffic has been an important Alaska business. A University of Alaska Anchorage study attributed more than 2,700 jobs in 1994 to existing international cargo activity at the Anchorage International Airport.
Flights involving the expanded cargo activities were expected to produce 2.5 times as much employment as cargo flights that land in Alaska merely for refueling, according to state estimates.

Until the late 1980s, Anchorage was a key refueling stop for passenger flights between Asia, Europe and North America. But the opening of Siberian airspace shortened international flights, reducing the need for polar routes and the new aircraft reduced refueling requirements.
